summary: The Foucault pendulum, devised by French physicist Léon Foucault in 1851, is a long, heavy pendulum whose plane of oscillation appears to rotate, giving simple direct evidence of the Earth's rotation. The note covers the original Panthéon experiment, the mechanics (rotation rate proportional to the sine of latitude), related precessing systems, notable pendulums worldwide, and the South Pole installation.
one_line: Léon Foucault's 1851 pendulum experiment showed Earth's rotation through the apparent rotation of its swing plane, with mechanics, history and notable installations.
key_facts: The Foucault pendulum was introduced in 1851 by Léon Foucault and was the first experiment to give simple, direct evidence of the Earth's rotation; he followed in 1852 with a gyroscope experiment.
The first public exhibition took place in February 1851 in the Meridian of the Paris Observatory.
Foucault's most famous pendulum used a 28-kilogram (62 lb) brass-coated lead bob on a 67-metre (220 ft) wire from the dome of the Panthéon, Paris.
At the Panthéon's latitude of 48°52'N, the swing plane made a full circle in about 31.8 h (31 h 50 min), rotating clockwise about 11.3° per hour.

The angular speed of the plane's precession is 360° times the sine of the latitude per sidereal day; at the equator the plane stays fixed relative to Earth, and at 30° south latitude it rotates counterclockwise 360° in two days.
At the North Pole the plane completes a full clockwise rotation in one day relative to Earth; at the South Pole it rotates counterclockwise.
On April 6, 2010, the cable holding the bob in the Musée des Arts et Métiers snapped, irreparably damaging the original bob and the marble floor.
An exact copy of the original pendulum has operated under the Panthéon dome since 1995.
Heike Kamerlingh Onnes (Nobel laureate 1913) performed precise experiments and developed a fuller theory of the pendulum for his 1879 doctoral thesis.
Vincenzo Viviani observed veering of a pendulum in 1661, but there is no evidence he connected it with the Earth's rotation.

The Oregon Convention Center pendulum is claimed to be the largest at about 27 m, though the Gamow Tower at the University of Colorado has one of 39.3 m, and Saint Isaac's Cathedral once had a 98 m pendulum.
At the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, a 33 m pendulum with a 25 kg bob confirmed a rotation period of about 24 hours.
